sections.title: The Blessing Is Over Enjoyment
sections.html:
The Sages instituted that the birkhot ha-nehenin (blessings over enjoyment) be recited over the enjoyment a person derives from his eating and drinking. Even if he eats or drinks only a minute amount, if he enjoys it he must recite a blessing, for "it is forbidden for a person to derive benefit from this world without a blessing" (Berakhot 35a). But one who does not enjoy it does not recite a blessing. Therefore, one who is completely full, to the point that he is repulsed by eating more, and nevertheless is compelled to eat, for example because he does not want to offend his hosts, should not recite a blessing over this eating, which is called 'akhila gasa' (gluttonous eating). But if, despite being full, he still has a sensation of enjoyment in his throat, he recites a blessing (MB 197:28).

The same law applies to water: since it has no taste, sometimes one who drinks it does not enjoy it with his palate. Therefore the Sages said that specifically "one who drinks water to quench his thirst recites a blessing" (Berakhot 44a), but if he drank it for another reason, since he did not enjoy it, he does not recite a blessing. For example, one who has food stuck in his throat and drinks water to wash it down, or who drinks a little water to help him swallow a medicinal pill, does not recite a blessing. But one who drinks juice to wash down food stuck in his throat or to help him swallow medicine, even though his main intention is to wash down the food or swallow the medicine, since the juice has a taste that he enjoys, he must recite a blessing (Berakhot 45a, Tosafot there; SA 204:7; MB 42).

Likewise, one who drinks water before a fast in order to store up fluids in his body ahead of the fast, or one who is about to set out on a journey and drinks water so that he will not be thirsty later, or one who suffers from constipation and drinks water so that he will be able to relieve himself, or a nursing mother who drinks water to increase her milk – as long as they have no enjoyment from the drinking, they should not recite a blessing. But if they drank juice for this purpose, or if they were thirsty and therefore enjoy the water, they recite a blessing.

One who eats a food or drinks a beverage for medicinal purposes: if it tastes bitter, he does not recite a blessing; and if it does not taste bad, even though he would not eat it were it not for the medical need, since his palate enjoys it somewhat, he recites a blessing. But one who sucks a pill that has some taste, since it is not a food, recites Shehakol only if he really enjoys the taste; and if he does not enjoy it, but the taste merely enables him to suck the pill without a feeling of disgust, he should not recite a blessing (SA 204:8; MB 43).

One who tastes a food only to know its taste, and afterward spits it out of his mouth, should not recite a blessing. Likewise, one who chews food for a baby, even though he senses its taste, does not recite a blessing. But one who chews gum must recite Shehakol, because his intention is to enjoy the taste, and this is an accepted manner of enjoyment. In addition, he also swallows the flavor components in the gum.1

sections.title: A Normal Manner of Enjoyment
sections.html:
The enjoyment of eating includes two components: the enjoyment of the palate from the taste of the food, and the enjoyment of the innards from its nutritional value, which gives a person strength and vitality. There are cases in which a person enjoys it in his innards but not in his throat, and then the law is that if he eats in the normal manner of eating, he must recite a blessing before eating.

For example, a sick person who is unable to sense the taste of food, since the food nourishes him, must recite a blessing. Likewise, when a person swallows his food without sensing its taste, since it nourishes him, he must recite a blessing. But a sick person who is fed through a tube (a feeding tube) that conveys his food into his stomach does not recite a blessing, neither before his eating nor after it. And even though he derives great benefit from it, for through it he receives the food necessary for his existence, since this is not the normal manner of eating, the enactment of the blessings does not apply to it. If he wishes to be scrupulous, he may thank God in a personal formulation.

One who eats a bitter or sour food whose taste is repellent, even though it is nourishing, should not recite a blessing, because it is not normal to eat things whose taste is repellent. Therefore one who drinks olive oil or vinegar, whose taste arouses revulsion, does not recite a blessing. Likewise, one who eats types of spices that, because of their great sourness or sharpness, people are not accustomed to eat on their own, does not recite a blessing. But one who personally enjoys the taste of the vinegar, the oil or the spices, since for him this is a normal manner of eating or drinking, recites Shehakol. And likewise the reverse: one who is compelled to eat a certain food that is repulsive to him, even though in the eyes of others it is considered good food, should not recite a blessing, since to him it is repulsive.2
A person who eats a food that tastes good to him but that nutritionally causes him more harm than benefit must recite a blessing, because in practice he enjoys it in the normal manner of eating. For example, a diabetic who eats cakes, or a heart patient who eats fatty food, or one who suffers from heartburn who eats fried food – even though the food may harm him, since he enjoys it in his throat and eats it in the normal manner of eating, he must recite a blessing. But one who eats a food that truly endangers his life should not recite a blessing, since it is forbidden for him to eat it.3

sections.title: Not Interrupting Between the Blessing and the Eating
sections.html:
The blessings that the Sages instituted to be said before a person enjoys his eating must be said immediately before the eating. One should not interrupt between the blessing and the eating or drinking even with silence; but a pause lasting less time than it takes to say three words, such as "Shalom alekha Rebbi" ("Peace be upon you, my teacher"), is not considered an interruption. In order not to interrupt between the blessing and the eating, one should first prepare the food and drink and only afterward recite the blessing over it. For example, one who wants to eat an orange should first peel it, and when it is ready to be eaten, recite the blessing over it. And one who wants to eat almonds or seeds should first crack the shell and only afterward recite the blessing. Likewise, one must be careful not to recite a blessing over tea that is so hot that he cannot drink it immediately and will have to wait between the blessing and the drinking.

All this is le-khatḥila (ideally), but be-di'avad (after the fact), if he recited the blessing and waited in silence between the blessing and the eating longer than the time it takes to say "Shalom alekha Rebbi", and even if during that time he hummed or made various sounds to hint something to his friend, as long as he did not divert his attention from the fact that he is between the blessing and the eating, he has not lost the blessing. But if he said even one word unrelated to the blessing and the eating, since he interrupted with speech, he has lost the blessing and must recite the blessing a second time in order to eat (SA 206:3; MB 12).

If he needs to say something urgent, he should wait until he has swallowed a little of the food or drink, and only afterward speak. And if he erred and spoke after he put the food in his mouth but before he swallowed any of it, there is a doubt whether he has fulfilled the obligation of the blessing. In practice, since the matter is disputed, he should not recite the blessing again, for in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient. But le-khatḥila one must be careful not to speak at all before swallowing something of the food or drink.4

If he erred and spoke between the blessing and the eating about a matter related to the food, he does not recite the blessing again. For example, if he recited a blessing over an apple and asked for a knife or asked whether it had been washed – although he acted improperly, for one should not speak at all between the blessing and the eating – since his speech was about a matter related to the eating, his speech does not separate between the blessing and the eating, and he need not recite the blessing a second time (SA and Rema OḤ 167:6; see above 3:3).

sections.title: How the Blessing Is Recited
sections.html:
One who recites a blessing over a food or a drink should preferably hold it in his hand at the time of the blessing, for in this way he will concentrate his heart more. It is proper to hold the food in the right hand, because it is more important (SA 206:4). As for a left-handed person, some say that since his dominant hand is the left, it is the honored one for him, and therefore he should hold the food in his left hand (MB 206:18). According to the custom of the kabbalists, even a left-handed person should hold the food in his right hand, which alludes to ḥesed (kindness) and should be given more honor (Ben Ish Ḥai, Shelaḥ 19). A person may choose his custom in this matter. But it seems that when a left-handed person recites a blessing for the public, as in Kiddush or Sheva Berakhot, it is preferable that he hold the cup in his right hand.

One should not recite a blessing over a food that is not in front of him. If he recited a blessing over something that is not in front of him, if there is certainty that he will eat from it, even though it is not in front of him, his blessing is a valid blessing. But if there is any concern that perhaps he will not taste the food, his blessing is in vain. For example, a person who knows with certainty about a food that is inside the cupboard and recited a blessing over it has fulfilled his obligation be-di'avad. But if he recited a blessing over a food that his friend is about to bring him, since it depends on his friend and there is no complete certainty in this, he has not fulfilled his obligation.

One who wants to drink water from the tap may recite the blessing and afterward open the flow of water; even though the water he will drink is not in front of him, since it is absolutely clear that the water will flow immediately upon opening the tap, it is considered as being in front of him (SA 206:5-6; MB 19).

When a person recites a blessing, his mouth must be empty of food. For example, if he ate a tree fruit and wants to eat a fruit of the ground, he should first finish swallowing all the fruit in his mouth, and only afterward recite the blessing over the fruit of the ground. For it is not in keeping with the honor of the blessing that it be said with a mouth that has food in it, as it is stated (Tehillim 71:8): "My mouth shall be filled with Your praise" (Berakhot 51a). Therefore he also should not recite the blessing in a slurred manner, but rather should say every word clearly (MB 172:7).

If he erred and put food in his mouth without a blessing, if he can take it out without it becoming repulsive, he should take it out of his mouth and recite the blessing. And if it would become repulsive when he takes it out of his mouth, he should move the food to one side of his mouth and recite the blessing. If he erred and put a drink in his mouth without a blessing, if he can move it to the side of his mouth and recite the blessing with difficulty, he should move it to the side of his mouth and recite the blessing. And if he cannot recite the blessing with the drink in his mouth, it is better that he spit it out, so as not to enjoy it without a blessing. If he needs it very much, he should swallow it without a blessing. Likewise, if spitting it out would arouse disgust in his companions, he should swallow it without a blessing (SA 172:1-2; MB 1-2).

sections.title: How Far a Blessing Exempts
sections.html:
If one recited Borei Pri Ha-etz over a fruit with the thought that he may want to eat more fruits from what is in his house, he has exempted all the fruits in his house, even though they are not in front of him on the table, and even though he did not know precisely which fruits he has. Likewise, one who is always accustomed, after eating one fruit, to take more fruits of different kinds, even if he did not think about this explicitly when he recited the blessing over the first fruit, has exempted all the fruits that he is accustomed to eat. And even if he is not always accustomed to eat more, if the fruits were in front of him at the time of the blessing, since a person sometimes gets drawn into eating more of what is in front of him, they are exempted by his blessing. The law regarding foods whose blessing is Shehakol, Ha-adama or Mezonot is the same as the law regarding tree fruit.5

But if he intended to eat only one fruit and no more, he has exempted only it, and if he wants to eat more fruits, he will have to recite a blessing again. Likewise, if he recited a blessing without any specific intention, and they brought him a fruit that he did not at all expect to be brought to him, for example they brought it from another house, he must recite a blessing over it (SA 177:5; 206:5; MB 206:20).

If one recited a blessing over a food without specific intention, neither intending to exempt all the kinds of foods that are exempted by that same blessing nor intending to eat only the food over which he recited the blessing, and afterward he wanted to eat more foods that are in his house and are not on his table, the poskim disagree whether they were exempted by his blessing. Since in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient, he should eat them without a blessing. Le-khatḥila it is proper always to intend, with every blessing one recites, to exempt all the foods and drinks in the house that have the same blessing (SA and Rema 206:5). One who has become accustomed to think this way is considered as one who intended it even on occasions when he forgot to intend it explicitly.6

sections.title: Hesesh Ha-da'at (Diversion of Attention)
sections.html:
If one recited a blessing over a food with the thought that perhaps he will want to continue eating from it and from foods exempted by his blessing, as long as he still intends to continue eating, even if he paused for the entire day, he may continue eating on the basis of his first blessing. But if he resolved in his mind not to eat any more, he has diverted his attention from the eating, and if afterward he changes his mind and wants to continue eating, he must again recite a first blessing over whatever he wishes to eat. The law for drinking is the same as for eating (Rambam, Hilkhot Berakhot 4:7).7

Sometimes a person is in a situation of doubtful 'hesesh ha-da'at' (diversion of attention), for example one who knows of himself that even after he decides not to eat any more, he is liable to change his mind. In such a situation, le-khatḥila it is preferable that he not eat any more; however, if he insists on continuing to eat, he should eat without a blessing, since perhaps the blessing he recited at first is still effective for him. And if he wants to continue eating and recite blessings without any doubts, he should recite an after-blessing over what he ate and leave his house for a very short walk, and when he returns, if he wants to continue eating, he should recite a blessing and eat.

A guest who thought they would not bring him any more food, and had already made up his mind not to eat any more, and afterward they brought him more food, since he relies on the intention of the host, may continue eating without reciting a blessing. And even if the host, too, had resolved in his heart not to eat any more, and then reconsidered and brought more food – although the host must recite a blessing over his new eating, the guest need not recite a blessing, for since he is a guest, he does not decide definitively to end his eating. Only if he made up his mind that even if they urge him to continue eating he will not eat, then if he wants to continue eating he will have to recite a first blessing again (SA 179:2, 5).

One who paused in the middle of his eating for prayer does not need to recite a blessing again when he returns to eat, because he did not divert his attention from continuing to eat (SA 178:6). Likewise, one who dozed off, even for an hour – this is not considered an interruption, and when he continues eating he does not recite a blessing again. But if he went to sleep a proper sleep in his bed (at least half an hour), it is as if he diverted his attention from the eating, and when he returns to eat he will have to recite a blessing before eating (SA 178:7; MB 48).

sections.title: Which Change of Place Requires a New Blessing
sections.html:
As we have learned, one who recited a blessing over a food, as long as he still intends to eat from it, even if he paused for the entire day, may continue eating on the basis of his first blessing. But if he changed his place, a great question arises whether he must recite a blessing again. In this law there is a difference between the kinds of foods.

Regarding foods over which one recites Birkat Ha-mazon or Me'ein Shalosh, since they are important foods, there is a doubt whether a change of place cancels the force of the first blessing. Therefore, le-khatḥila, one who wishes to continue eating them should not change his place, and if he did change it, it is preferable that he not continue eating. And if he insists on continuing to eat, he should not recite a blessing, for in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient (and what constitutes a change of place will be explained below regarding the second kind of foods).8
But regarding foods over which one recites Borei Nefashot, according to all opinions, if he changed his place the force of the first blessing has lapsed, and if he wants to continue eating he will be obligated to recite a first blessing again. Since there is no doubt in this law, whenever he needs to change his place, he may do so and recite a first blessing again. However, it must be explained what constitutes a change of place that requires a new blessing:

One who is eating in one room inside his home and wants to go to another room, or to a balcony, or to his private yard – if he planned from the outset to move there, or if these are places he is sometimes accustomed to go to while eating, he may le-khatḥila go to them and continue eating without a blessing, because for him this is not considered a change of place. And if it is a room, balcony, stairwell or private yard to which he is not accustomed to go while eating or drinking, le-khatḥila he should not go to them, and if he went, since they are subsidiary to his home, he need not recite a blessing anew (see BHL 178:1, s.v. "be-bayit eḥad").

But if he went out to the street or to another house, even if from the outset he intended to continue his eating there, since he changed his place, if he wants to continue eating he must recite a blessing (and see MB 178:12, 39; BHL 1, s.v. "le-fetaḥ beito").

If, when he went out, his friend who was eating with him remained in the place of their eating or drinking, his friend has preserved his connection to the place of eating and to the first blessing, and when he returns he may continue eating and drinking without a blessing. In case of need one may act this way even le-khatḥila (SA 178:2).

One who ate outdoors, as long as he can see the place where he originally recited the blessing, is still considered not to have changed his place.

A special law applies to travelers: the whole road is their place, and therefore a change of place is not considered an interruption for them (SA 178:4; MB 42).

sections.title: The Order of Precedence Among Different Blessings
sections.html:
When a person has in front of him several foods whose blessings differ, it is proper to be scrupulous and recite blessings over them according to the order of importance that the Sages stated. For just as a person who is about to speak before an important minister plans his words well – what he will open with and what he will continue with – so one who is about to recite blessings before the King of kings ought to say his blessings in the perfect order. Two rules were stated regarding the order of blessings: first, that one should first recite the blessing over the more important food; and second, that one should first recite the more specific blessing, that is, the blessing directed to a special and specific kind of food.

According to this, it is clear that the blessing over bread takes precedence over all, since bread is the most important food. When there is no intention to eat bread, the order of importance among the blessings is: Mezonot, Gefen (wine), Etz (tree fruit), Adama (fruit of the ground), Shehakol [the Hebrew acronym is "magaʿ ash"].

The Mezonot blessing is more important than the other blessings, because Mezonot foods are the most satiating. (Therefore, at the time of Kiddush, the ḥalla and the Mezonot foods are covered, so that it will not appear that one is giving wine precedence over bread and Mezonot; see Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 6:8.)

After that, the blessing over wine is the important one, for since wine nourishes and satiates, the Sages instituted a special blessing for it (Rema 211:4-5).

After that, the blessings over fruits – Ha-etz and Ha-adama – take precedence over Shehakol, since they are more specific, for they are intended only for fruits, whereas Shehakol is a general blessing for all other foods.

Among the blessings over fruits, Ha-etz takes precedence over Ha-adama, since Ha-etz is more specific, for be-di'avad, if one recited Ha-adama over a tree fruit he has fulfilled his obligation, whereas if he recited Ha-etz over a fruit of the ground he has not fulfilled his obligation. However, regarding the blessings over fruits there are several more rules – that one should give preference to the favored fruit and to fruits of the seven species – and we will detail them in halakha 10.

The orders of precedence among the blessings apply on condition that both kinds of food are placed in front of him and he wants to eat both of them now. But if one is in front of him and the other is in the cupboard – for example, he has fruits in front of him, and afterward he intends to bring Mezonot and wine – he may le-khatḥila first recite the blessing over the fruits, and afterward, when he brings the Mezonot and the wine, recite blessings over them. Likewise, one who was served vegetable soup and ptitim (pasta flakes), and according to his order of eating he wants to begin by eating the vegetable soup, since at the moment he does not wish to eat from both, he may first recite Ha-adama over the vegetable soup, and afterward recite Mezonot over the ptitim (Ritva; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 249, Kuntres Aḥaron 4).

sections.title: The Order of Precedence Among Identical Blessings
sections.html:
One who wants to eat several kinds of food whose blessing is the same should properly say the blessing over the more important food, for this is the honor of the blessing, that it be said over the important food, and thereby it will exempt the other foods whose blessing is the same.

There are several rules of importance: a) A whole food takes precedence over a cut one; therefore one who recites a blessing over cookies, and there is a whole cookie and a broken one, should recite the blessing over the whole one. b) The favored one takes precedence: if there were two cookies of different kinds, he should recite the blessing over the cookie he likes more. c) The large takes precedence over the small: if he had two cookies that he wants to eat, both whole and equally favored, and one is larger, he should recite the blessing over the larger one.

Likewise, with kinds of meat and fish whose blessing is Shehakol, the whole takes precedence over the cut, the favored over the less favored, and the large over the small.

When there is a conflict between these rules, the first rule takes precedence over the second, and the second over the third. For example, if he has a whole cookie that is less favored, and on the other hand a broken cookie that is favored, it is preferable that he recite the blessing over the whole one.9

sections.title: The Order of Precedence in the Blessings over Fruits and the Praise of the Land of Israel
sections.html:
The Torah mentioned seven species in praise of the Land of Israel, as it is stated (Devarim 8:7-8): "For the Lord your God is bringing you into a good land … a land of wheat and barley, and vines and figs and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey." Since these species were mentioned in praise, when a person is about to eat two kinds of fruit, it is a mitzva for him to recite the blessing over the fruit for which the Land of Israel was praised, and with his blessing he exempts the other kind. For example, if they brought him grapes and apples, he should recite the blessing over the grapes and with their blessing exempt the apples.

If he had in front of him two kinds from the seven species, he should recite the blessing over the one closer to the word 'land' (eretz), for whatever is closer to 'land' is more important. Therefore the order of precedence is as follows: olive, date, grapes, fig and pomegranate.

If he had in front of him two kinds of fruit, one from the seven species and the other not from the seven species but more favored by him: according to the Rambam, it is better that he recite the blessing over the fruit he favors, for since he favors it, the thanksgiving over it is more significant from his perspective. However, according to most poskim, it is better to recite the blessing over the fruit for which the Land of Israel was praised. And this is the preferable practice (SA 211:1-2; MB 211:33).10

If he had in front of him fruits of the ground and tree fruits: if both are equally favored by him, we have already learned (halakha 8) that it is preferable to recite the blessing over the tree fruit first, because its blessing is more specific. All the more so, if one of the fruits is of the seven species, if they are equally favored, he should first recite the blessing over the fruit of the seven species. But if the fruit of the ground is more favored by him, even though the tree fruit is of the seven species, it is preferable to recite the blessing first over the fruit of the ground, for since it does not exempt the tree fruit with its blessing, it is better that he first recite the blessing over what he favors more.11
